Expectation1: Help out during difficult times or emergencies.
Situation1: A friend on their way to the airport calls, thinking they left their passport at home, and asks if you can check and bring it to them right away.
Expectation2: Fix bugs and troubleshoot issues reported by users or QA
Situation2: A production outage traces back to a defect in their code and customers cannot access the service
Story: My phone buzzes just as I’m about to dive into the error logs. It’s Sam, frantic—he’s on his way to the airport and thinks he left his passport at home. “Can you check and bring it? I’ll miss my flight otherwise,” he pleads. I glance at my screen: the production outage alert is still flashing, and Slack is blowing up with messages from QA and my manager. Customers can’t log in, and the root cause points straight to my last commit. My heart pounds. Sam’s counting on me—he’s never asked for help like this before. But the team is waiting, and every minute the service is down, more users are locked out. I can almost hear the disappointment in both their voices, whichever way I turn. My hands tremble as I weigh the urgency of a friend in crisis against the responsibility to my team and our users.
